# AppraisalScope / Cotality Digital Gateway — the vendor's own client package

This is the integration package AppraisalScope ships to a client, saved here so the
request and response shapes we build against are in the repository rather than in
somebody's downloads folder (owner-directed 2026-08-16: *"save this zip file also into
the repo so it should be available as knowledge and a resource"*).

It is **reference material only** — nothing at runtime reads any of it.

## What is here

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `iPackage_AppraisalScope_Client_2024-09-27.zip` | The package as delivered, one value redacted (below) |
| `samples/` | The same sample request/response bodies, unpacked so they are greppable and diffable |
| `Postman/` | The vendor's Postman collection + a blank environment |

`samples/` and `Postman/` are unpacked copies of what is inside the zip. They exist so a
change to our request builders can be diffed against the vendor's own example in a code
review; the zip exists so the package can be handed on intact.

## THE ONE THING THAT WAS CHANGED

Every sample in this package carries a working **UAT API key** — the vendor's own demo
credential for the `integrations.uat` sandbox — as the `ApiKey` reference identifier.
It appears in 25 files.

It has been replaced everywhere, **inside the zip as well as in the unpacked copies**,
with the placeholder `{{api_key}}`. Nothing else was touched: same files, same
directory structure, same bytes otherwise.

That is deliberate and is the repo's standing rule — a credential never goes into a
tracked file, and "it is only the vendor's sandbox key" is not an exception worth
making, because a key committed once stays in the history forever. The placeholder is
also the more useful value: it is exactly what the Postman collection expects, so the
samples work as templates rather than as one particular tenant's snapshot.

For provenance, the **unmodified** archive's checksum was
`782b30623bafb5c80e0dc0b77e156c2653e502f4c5a7d7dcdc205249d7ea3cac`
(sha256). The copy here is a rebuild of that archive with the redaction applied, so its
own checksum differs — that is expected, not corruption.

**Our real API key is never in this repository.** It comes from the environment
(`AMC_API_KEY`, see `src/config.js`) and is set in the Render dashboard.

## Everything else in here is already safe to read

- The card numbers in the payment samples (`4012888888881881`, `4111…`) are the
  publicly published Visa test PANs, not anybody's card.
- The Postman environment file ships blank — no host, no key, no password.
- The addresses, borrower names and order numbers are the vendor's own fixtures.

## What the payment samples tell us

The reason this package was pulled in is `Samples/Orders/`, which is the only written
statement of how AppraisalScope wants a card charged. Three details in there are ones
the sample bodies alone would have got wrong, so they are worth stating in prose:

1. **`paymentReferenceIdentifier` is generated by the CLIENT** — it is our handle for
   the payment, not something the vendor hands back first.
2. **`PaymentAuthCapture` carries no amount.** The fee is the one already agreed on the
   order; sending a number would imply we get to choose it.
3. **The security code (`paymentAccountCardSecurityCode`) is required** on
   `PaymentAuthCapture`. The later `PaymentCapture` — against a card the vendor has
   already vaulted — takes only the payment reference and the cardholder's email, and
   needs no card number and no security code.

The response to a successful charge carries
`message.products[0].payments[0].paymentTransactionId`, which is the receipt to record
against the order.
